article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Sativa-leaning hybrid
Genetics: Tangie × Guava Dawg
Breeder: Growing Passion / Brett Wilson
THC Content: 16–20%
CBD Content: Typically below 1%
Terpene Profile: myrcene , ocimene, caryophyllene
Primary Flavors: Orange, tangerine, guava, tropical fruit
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8–9 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: early October
Indoor Yield: Moderate to potentially high
Outdoor Yield: Moderate to high
Grow Difficulty: Intermediate

Passion Orange Guava is one of those cannabis strains whose name sounds exaggerated until a properly grown flower is opened. Citrus arrives immediately, often closer to freshly crushed tangerine peel than generic lemon, followed by ripe tropical fruit, guava-like sweetness, mango, and a sharper diesel note underneath. The contrast is important. Without the fuel, earth, and sour funk supplied by the Dawg side of the pedigree, the weed could easily become another uncomplicated fruit strain. Instead, its aroma moves between bright orange juice and pungent Chem-style gas, giving the cultivar considerably more depth than its tropical name implies.

The original POG is associated with Santa Cruz breeder Brett Wilson, better known through the Growing Passion name. Wilson later collaborated with Berner on the development of the Lemonnade brand, and contemporary reporting specifically identifies him as the Santa Cruz breeder behind Growing Passion. Passion Orange Guava predates many of today’s candy-dominant hybrids and reflects a slightly different breeding philosophy: Tangie’s intense citrus terpenes were paired with the tropical, chemical funk of Guava Dawg to produce marijuana that remains lively, aromatic, and strongly connected to classic California sativa culture.
Genetics and Lineage

Tangie provides the unmistakable orange side of the family. DNA Genetics documents Tangie as California Orange crossed with Skunk #1 , creating a sativa-leaning cultivar recognized for tangerine peel, citrus oil, earth, and an energetic cerebral profile. California Orange gives the parent its juicy orange core, while Skunk adds vigor, pungency, and an earthy backdrop. In Passion Orange Guava, those characteristics remain remarkably easy to identify, especially in phenotypes that release an almost concentrated orange-rind aroma when the flowers are broken apart.

Guava Dawg brings a very different genetic personality. The cultivar is associated with Top Dawg Genetics and combines Afghani #1 , Stardawg , and Tres Dawg ancestry, giving it substantial Chem-family influence. An earlier independent strain profile describes Guava Dawg as Stardawg × Tres Dawg × Afghani #1 and emphasizes its combination of Chem fuel with tropical fruit sweetness. That parent contributes guava, mango, apricot-like fruit, diesel, earth, and a heavier physical side to the POG family.

Put together, the lineage explains why Passion Orange Guava does not behave like a pure Tangie offspring. The citrus is unmistakable, but the Guava Dawg side adds density to both aroma and effects. Orange, tropical fruit, and bright sweetness sit on top, while sour fuel, spice, earth, and Chem-like funk emerge underneath. Even the high reflects both sides: Tangie pushes the experience upward and outward, while Guava Dawg keeps the body from feeling completely weightless.
Effects and Experience

The onset is generally quick and mentally noticeable. Moderate amounts can bring a clear rise in mood, stronger sensory engagement, and a feeling of forward momentum that makes the cultivar well suited to music, conversation, errands, creative work, or social settings. Thoughts may feel more fluid, and the environment can become more interesting without immediately producing the haziness associated with heavier weed. That energetic quality is one reason POG is commonly treated as a daytime or afternoon strain.

Focus can be present early, but the experience is not always perfectly linear. With additional THC, that concentration may loosen into more spontaneous or scattered thinking. Conversation becomes easier, ideas can branch rapidly, and some consumers may feel more talkative than task-oriented. This progression distinguishes Passion Orange Guava from strains that deliver narrow, almost caffeine-like stimulation. It feels more euphoric and exploratory than purely functional.

The body component remains comparatively light at moderate intake. A gentle relaxation can develop through the shoulders and limbs without eliminating the cerebral energy, creating a balanced middle phase. Larger amounts make the Guava Dawg influence more obvious, potentially bringing stronger physical calm, appetite stimulation, and mental cloudiness. Dry mouth and dry eyes are common THC-related drawbacks, while consumers sensitive to stimulating cannabis may experience racing thoughts, restlessness, or anxiety if they exceed their comfortable dose.
Medical Benefits

Passion Orange Guava has not been evaluated as an individual medical marijuana treatment in controlled clinical trials. Claims that the strain treats specific conditions therefore go beyond the available evidence. Its subjective profile may nevertheless appeal to medical cannabis consumers who prefer an uplifting cultivar rather than one that immediately produces heavy sedation.

A brighter mood and increased mental energy may be attractive to patients using cannabis during the daytime, while the later body relaxation can provide a softer physical component without necessarily ending productivity. Appetite can also increase as the experience progresses. People seeking temporary relief from stress, low appetite, mild discomfort, or fatigue may find this style of THC-dominant cannabis appealing, but individual responses vary considerably.

Patients prone to anxiety should be cautious. Sativa-leaning strains with prominent cerebral effects can become uncomfortable at high doses even when the same flower feels pleasant in smaller amounts. The best medical reference is the certificate of analysis from the exact batch being consumed, including THC, minor cannabinoids, and terpene concentrations. A strain name alone cannot predict an individual therapeutic response.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Orange is the centerpiece, but the best POG flower goes considerably further. Freshly opened buds can smell like tangerine peel, sweet orange juice, tropical nectar, and ripe guava. Mango and apricot-like fruit may appear in the background, especially once the flower warms in the hand. The Tangie parent gives the bouquet its high, bright citrus notes, while Guava Dawg makes the lower portion of the aroma darker and more pungent.

Grinding the buds changes the profile. Sour citrus becomes sharper, and diesel, skunk, damp earth, and chemical funk begin cutting through the fruit. This is where the cultivar’s Chem and Dawg ancestry becomes most obvious. A strong phenotype can move from almost breakfast-juice sweetness into an aroma resembling citrus rind rubbed against fuel and soil.

The flavor usually begins with orange and tropical fruit before turning earthier on the exhale. Tangerine zest can leave a slight bitterness similar to actual citrus peel, while guava and mango add softer sweetness through the middle. Diesel and herbal spice linger afterward. Depending on the phenotype, myrcene can deepen the tropical and earthy qualities, caryophyllene can add pepper, ocimene may contribute brighter herbal sweetness, and limonene can reinforce the citrus impression. Exact terpene concentrations should still be verified by laboratory testing rather than assumed from aroma.
Growing Information

Detailed original breeder cultivation specifications for Passion Orange Guava are difficult to document today, so precise yield claims should be approached cautiously. Cultivation reports generally describe a medium-to-tall plant with the stretch expected from Tangie ancestry. Indoor flowering is often placed around eight to nine weeks, though individual phenotypes may require additional time. Because the original breeder does not maintain a widely available standardized cultivation chart for the strain, trichome maturity and flower development are better harvest indicators than a fixed day count.

The sativa-influenced architecture makes early training useful indoors. Topping can encourage several main branches rather than a dominant central stem, while low-stress training or a screen can spread the canopy beneath available lighting. Stretch should be anticipated when flowering begins. Growers with limited vertical space should establish the desired plant structure before the transition rather than trying to control excessive height late in bloom.

Flower clusters tend to retain enough openness that airflow can move through the canopy, but humidity still deserves attention as resin production increases. Strong light and healthy roots can help the plant develop more substantial colas, while excessive nitrogen late in flowering may interfere with aroma and maturation. The citrus profile is particularly sensitive to post-harvest handling. Drying too rapidly or at high temperatures can strip away volatile orange and tropical notes, leaving a flatter earthy-diesel profile behind.

Outdoor growers can take advantage of the plant’s vigor where summers are warm and autumn conditions remain reasonably dry. Early October is a useful general target in many Northern Hemisphere gardens, although latitude, phenotype, and seasonal weather can shift harvest considerably. Plants given unrestricted root space may become substantially larger than indoor specimens, making branch support worthwhile as flowers gain weight.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Passion Orange Guava?
The original Passion Orange Guava is Tangie × Guava Dawg. Tangie contributes California Orange and Skunk genetics, while Guava Dawg adds Afghani, Stardawg, Tres Dawg, and Chem-family ancestry.
Who bred Passion Orange Guava?

The original cultivar is associated with Santa Cruz breeder Brett Wilson, known as Growing Passion. Wilson is independently documented as the breeder behind Growing Passion and later collaborated with Berner on California cannabis projects.
Is Passion Orange Guava indica or sativa?

It is best described as a sativa-leaning hybrid. Tangie strongly influences the early cerebral and energetic effects, while Guava Dawg provides a more grounded physical component as the high develops.
What does Passion Orange Guava taste like?
Expect orange, tangerine, guava, mango, tropical fruit, sour citrus, diesel, and earth. The brightest examples can resemble fresh orange peel and tropical juice before finishing with Chem-like fuel.
How strong is Passion Orange Guava?

Traditional flower is commonly reported in roughly the upper-teens to around 20% THC range, though modern cultivation can produce different results. The laboratory label from the specific batch should always be used instead of assuming one fixed potency.
Final Thoughts on Passion Orange Guava

Passion Orange Guava stands out because its tropical identity is rooted in recognizable genetics rather than a flavor-driven marketing name. Tangie provides the intense orange peel, cerebral lift, and California sativa character, while Guava Dawg contributes tropical sweetness, Chem fuel, earth, and enough physical weight to make the experience feel complete. The resulting marijuana can be bright without feeling thin and fruity without becoming overly sugary.

Its aroma remains the main attraction. Few strains combine tangerine, guava, mango, sour citrus, and diesel so naturally, and the contrast becomes even stronger once the flower is ground. The flavor has enough sweetness for fruit-focused consumers but retains the skunk and fuel qualities that appeal to people who prefer older-school cannabis.

For daytime or early-evening consumers, POG can offer an especially useful progression: an energetic cerebral beginning, a more social or creative middle, and a gentler body relaxation toward the finish. Growers also have worthwhile traits to explore, particularly citrus intensity, branching vigor, resin production, and the balance between Tangie brightness and Guava Dawg funk. More than a decade after its creation, Passion Orange Guava remains a distinctive example of Santa Cruz breeding built around flavor, energy, and classic California cannabis genetics.
